Wherewithal
wair-with-AWL
adverb
A compound of where + with + all, meaning “with what.” Like whereby, wherein, and wherefore, it is an interrogative or relative adverb: wherewithal shall we be clothed? means with what shall we be clothed? As a noun it later came to mean the means or resources for a thing.

Biblical Definition

In the KJV wherewithal is an adverb meaning “with what” — a plain old member of the family of whereby, wherein, and wherefore. The modern reader knows the word only as a noun for money or means (“he hasn’t the wherewithal”), and so may stumble over its true and older use as a question: with what? Our Lord uses it so in forbidding anxious care: “Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” (Mat 6:31) — that is, with what shall we be clothed? He does not scold the question but the anxiety behind it, for the heavenly Father knows His children have need of these things. The Psalmist asks the same form of a holier matter: “Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way?” (Psa 119:9) — with what shall he make it clean? — and answers on the instant, “by taking heed thereto according to thy word.” The kindred word wherewith carries the same sense when Micah cries, “Wherewith shall I come before the LORD?” (Mic 6:6), and runs through his rising offers — rams, rivers of oil, even the firstborn (Mic 6:7) — only to be answered that the LORD requires justice, mercy, and a humble walk. So the word asks the great questions of life: wherewithal to be fed, cleansed, and brought before God. And Scripture gives its reply: the Word cleanses, the Father provides, and Christ alone brings us in.

Webster 1828 Definition

An adverb meaning ‘with what’; only later a noun for means or resources.

expand to see more

WHEREWITHAL, adv., with what; used interrogatively and relatively.

A compound of where + with + all, kin to whereby and wherein.

“Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” means “with what shall we be clothed?”

The Psalmist asks wherewithal a young man shall cleanse his way (Psa 119:9).

Only later did it become a noun meaning the means or money for a thing.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:31 — "Therefore take no thought, saying, What shall we eat? or, What shall we drink? or, Wherewithal shall we be clothed?"

Psa 119:9 — "BETH. Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? by taking heed thereto according to thy word."

Mic 6:6 — "Wherewith shall I come before the LORD, and bow myself before the high God? shall I come before him with burnt offerings, with calves of a year old?"

Mic 6:7 — "Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?"

Modern Corruption

An old adverb for ‘with what’ now known only as a noun for money — the question mistaken for the means.

expand to see more

The drift here is a change of part of speech. In the AV wherewithal is an adverb asking “with what?”; in modern usage it survives only as a noun meaning resources, chiefly money — “the wherewithal to do it.” So the reader who meets “Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” may hear a fragment or a puzzle, when it is a plain question: with what shall we be clothed? Restore the adverb and Christ’s words fall into order beside “what shall we eat” and “what shall we drink” — three anxious questions He bids His people lay down at the feet of a Father who feeds the birds.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that grammatical shift. The principle to recover is that the deepest wherewithals are not in our hands to supply. The world spends itself answering the lesser question — wherewithal shall we be clothed, housed, fed — and forgets the greater: wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? Micah’s escalating offers show the natural heart’s guess, that we must find the wherewithal ourselves, heaping up sacrifice until even the firstborn is on the altar. But no rivers of oil can cleanse a way; the Psalmist’s answer is the Word, and the gospel’s answer is the blood of Christ. The means of our cleansing was never ours to muster. God Himself has provided the wherewithal, and bids us take no anxious thought, but seek first His kingdom.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means ‘with what,’ a compound of where, with, and all.

expand to see more

Wherewithal — a compound of where + with + all, “with what.”

Kin to whereby, wherein, wherefore — the old adverb family.

“Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” (Mat 6:31) means “with what?”

The kindred wherewith asks the same: “Wherewith shall I come before the LORD?” (Mic 6:6).

Only later did it harden into a noun meaning means or money.

Usage

"“Wherewithal shall we be clothed?” simply asks, with what shall we be clothed?"

"Wherewithal shall a young man cleanse his way? By heeding God’s Word."

"The modern noun (“the wherewithal”) hides the old adverb, “with what.”"
